oil.summary: Brent held above $104/bbl despite a modest -0.98% day-over-day slip, as competing forces pulled in opposite directions. Saudi Arabia's decision to reroute crude exports via Oman eased immediate Hormuz choke-point fears and pressured crude lower intraday, while late-session reports of Chinese diplomatic pressure on Iran to rein in the Houthis added a de-escalation narrative. The products complex took a harder hit: RBOB fell 6.77% and Heating Oil dropped 6.87% on the day, though both remain significantly elevated on the month. Goldman Sachs flagged diesel-to-gasoline switching risk for refiners, while Kpler's Matt Smith argued six-plus months of Middle East supply losses will keep crude grinding higher. A Ukraine strike on a Moscow-area refinery co-owned by Rosneft and Gazprom Neft complicates the Russian product export picture, with Moscow reportedly set to extend its diesel export ban. CME options imply a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Saudi Arabia rerouting exports via Oman and China pressing Iran on Houthis provided intraday de-escalation relief, pressuring crude and products sharply lower
Ukraine drone strike on Moscow-area Rosneft/Gazprom Neft refinery and Russia's looming diesel export ban extension tighten the global distillate supply outlook
StanChart and Kpler maintain bullish medium-term floor view as Hormuz disruption effects continue to ripple through refined product markets

gas.summary: Henry Hub edged up 1.07% to $2.922/MMBtu, extending a steady weekly and monthly grind higher. TTF slipped 1.30% on the day to €77.015/MWh but remains up over 21% on the month, reflecting persistently low European storage levels and fierce competition for LNG spot cargoes amid the Hormuz supply crunch. Analysts cited by Reuters warned that soaring LNG prices are set to push Asian demand down 3–10% for a second consecutive annual decline. One analyst flagged LNG prices could still rise a further one-third from already elevated levels. On the supply risk side, Russia abruptly cut gas flows to Armenia days after Yerevan announced diversification plans — a pointed political signal. UK household energy bills are forecast to jump 25–30% in Q1 2027 if the Middle East crisis persists. India separately pushed back on US tariff threats over its continued Russian energy purchases.
drivers: Hormuz supply disruption sustaining fierce Europe-Asia LNG spot competition, with analysts warning prices could rise a further third from current elevated levels
Russia cutting gas to Armenia immediately after its diversification announcement underscores continued use of energy as a geopolitical lever
UK Q1 2027 household bills forecast up 25–30%, illustrating downstream demand destruction risk as TTF remains more than 21% above last month's levels

power.summary: EU Carbon EUAs ticked up a modest 0.59% to $81.62/EUA, holding a steady one-month uptrend of +5.45% that broadly tracks the elevated TTF gas price environment. TTF's own 1.30% day-over-day pullback provided some relief on the gas-to-power generation cost side, though the monthly gain of 21% keeps power generation margins under pressure across Europe. The headline risk for the power sector today came from the renewables space: Europe's largest independent solar operator filed for bankruptcy, attributed to unsustainable project economics in Germany driven by soaring wind and solar capacity buildout and slower-than-expected demand growth. Data flow for this sector is otherwise thin today beyond the cross-cutting gas price and Iran/Russia geopolitical threads.
drivers: EUA carbon prices holding a steady monthly uptrend, underpinned by elevated gas-fired generation costs as TTF remains 21% above last month
Europe's biggest independent solar operator declared bankruptcy, citing deteriorating project economics from overcapacity in Germany's renewables sector
Ongoing Hormuz disruption and Russian supply leverage keep European power fuel-cost uncertainty elevated heading into the winter demand season
